text.short: Grove Street between Sixth and Capitol, Boise. A pub, a market, a dining room, a club and a museum — and the museum is the boarding house all of it came out of.

sections.heading: One block, five doors
sections.body: Bar Gernika on the Capitol corner. The Basque Market halfway down, cooking paella on the pavement on Wednesdays and Fridays. Leku Ona at the Sixth Street end, with a hotel over it. The Basque Center, which is the club. And the Basque Museum & Cultural Center, in the Cyrus Jacobs-Uberuaga house.

sections.heading: The house came first
sections.body: Cyrus Jacobs built it in 1864. It became a Basque boarding house, the Uberuagas ran it from 1917 and owned it from 1928, and it took boarders until 1969. Sixteen years later Adelia Simplot opened a museum in it. The block assembled itself around a building that had been feeding Basque men for half a century.

sections.heading: What this does to a dinner for two
sections.body: In Winnemucca or Gardnerville the boarding house is the restaurant, so the long table comes with the meal. On the Basque Block the boarding house is a museum, and the restaurants beside it seat you at your own table. Same descent, different arrangement — and two people who want a room to themselves will find one more easily on Grove Street than on Highway 395.

sections.heading: Every five years it fills up
sections.body: Jaialdi runs six days and draws 30,000 to 50,000 people to these streets. The last was 29 July to 3 August 2025; the next is 2030. Anyone planning a quiet dinner in Boise that week should know it.
